problem: Every department in a company produces documents that need to live somewhere shared: CEx escalation templates, refund policy references, KYC procedure documents, training materials, scorecards, and audit evidence. If each agent kept their own copies on their own laptop, the business would lose consistency immediately — two agents referencing 'the KYC checklist' could be looking at two different, possibly outdated, versions, and if a laptop dies, whatever lived only on that machine is gone.

A file server solves this by giving the organization one authoritative, centrally managed place for shared files — with permissions controlling who can see what, versioning/backup protecting against loss, and a single source of truth that doesn't depend on any one person's machine. It's unglamorous infrastructure, but it's the reason 'the shared drive' or 'the department folder' works the same way for every employee, every day, without anyone thinking about how.
Why this matters at FundedNext specifically
CEx procedure documents, scorecard templates, and escalation matrices need to be identical for every agent on every shift — a file server (not individual laptops) is what guarantees that.

KYC and refund-related evidence often needs to be retained, access-controlled, and auditable — properties that only a centrally managed file server with proper permissions and logging can reliably provide.

The internally built Google Apps Script CEx application already centralizes data in Google Sheets rather than local files — the same underlying principle (one authoritative shared source instead of scattered personal copies) is exactly what an on-prem file server provides for documents instead of structured data.
concept: A file server is a server whose primary role is storing files and making them available to other machines over the network, along with enforcing who is allowed to read, write, or modify each file or folder. The two protocols that do the actual work of 'network access to files' are SMB (Server Message Block — the Windows-native protocol, used by \\server\share paths) and NFS (Network File System — the traditional Unix/Linux equivalent).

In a Windows/Active Directory environment (the dominant model in most enterprises, including FundedNext's likely setup), file shares are backed by NTFS permissions at the filesystem level and SMB share permissions at the network level — the two layers combine, and the more restrictive of the two always wins. Access is typically granted not to individual users directly but to AD security groups (Session 22), which is what makes permission management sane at scale.
Core vocabulary you need at this level Term Meaning Share A folder published over the network with a name (e.g., \\fs01\CEx-Docs) that clients connect to.
NTFS permissions Filesystem-level access control on the actual folder/file (Read, Write, Modify, Full Control, etc.), enforced regardless of how the file is accessed.
Share permissions Network-level access control applied only when accessing the folder via the share path; combines with NTFS permissions, most restrictive wins.
DFS (Distributed File System) A layer that lets multiple physical shares on different servers appear under one unified namespace/path, and can replicate content between sites.
Quota A limit on how much storage a user or folder is allowed to consume.
Shadow Copy / Previous Versions Point-in-time snapshots of a volume that let users restore an earlier version of a file themselves, without IT intervention.
deep: 3.1 SMB protocol basics SMB (now typically SMB 3.x in modern Windows environments) is the protocol behind every \\server\ share connection. Modern versions add encryption in transit, multichannel support (using multiple network paths simultaneously for throughput/resilience), and signing to prevent tampering — a considerable evolution from the much older, insecure SMB1, which most enterprises now disable entirely due to its association with exploits like EternalBlue/WannaCry.

3.2 NTFS permissions vs. share permissions, worked through This is the single most commonly misunderstood mechanic in file server administration. A user accessing a folder over the network is subject to both the share permission and the NTFS permission on that folder — whichever is more restrictive determines the effective access.

Share permission NTFS permission Effective access when accessed via the network share Full Control Read Only Read Only (NTFS is more restrictive) Read Only Full Control Read Only (Share is more restrictive) Full Control Full Control Full Control Read Only Read Only Read Only Best practice in most enterprises is to leave share permissions wide open (Everyone / Authenticated Users: Full Control at the share level) and do all the real, granular access control with NTFS permissions and AD security groups — this avoids the confusing 'two layers fighting each other' problem and keeps permission management in one place.

3.3 DFS Namespaces and DFS Replication DFS Namespaces let \\fundednext.local\CEx-Docs point transparently to a share on whichever server is actually hosting it — users never need to know or care which physical server their files live on, and IT can migrate or fail over the underlying server without changing anything users see. DFS Replication keeps copies of that data in sync across multiple servers/sites, so a branch office can have a local, fast copy of shared files that's kept consistent with the main site.
workflow: A step-by-step view of what actually happens when a new departmental share is created for CEx:
1. Identify the business need and owner — e.g., 'CEx needs a shared folder for escalation templates and scorecards, owned by the CEx team lead.'
2. Create AD security groups reflecting the intended access model (e.g., CEx-Agents-ReadOnly, CEx- Leads-Modify) rather than assigning permissions to individuals directly.
3. Create the folder on the file server, set NTFS permissions using those groups, and keep share permissions permissive (Section 3.2).
4. Publish the share into the existing DFS namespace so users access it via a consistent, location- independent path.
5. Enable Shadow Copies on the volume so users can self-service restore earlier versions of a file without a help desk ticket.
6. Set a quota if appropriate, to prevent one team or user from consuming disproportionate storage.
7. Confirm the share is included in the backup schedule (Session 78) and document its owner, purpose, and permission model.
8. Periodically audit group membership and permissions — access that made sense when the share was created can silently become wrong as people change roles, which is a common audit finding.
enterprise: File servers sit at Layer 5 (Enterprise Services), typically running on dedicated Windows Server (or Linux/Samba) instances with attached or SAN/NAS-backed storage (Session 77, later in this layer). They depend heavily on Layer 4 Identity — Active Directory is what supplies both the users and the security groups that all file permissions are ultimately built on — which is why file servers are one of the clearest examples of how the layers of this knowledge map build on each other in practice.

In a typical CEx-style enterprise topology, one or more file servers (often clustered or backed by highly available NAS storage) sit in the core/server VLAN, published through a DFS namespace, with departmental shares like CEx-Docs, CEx-Scorecards, and CEx-Training each carrying their own group- based permission model.
dependencies: What a file server itself needs in order to function correctly:
Active Directory (Sessions 51–52) for user authentication and the security groups permissions are built on.
DNS (Session 67) so clients can resolve the server name or DFS namespace path.
Kerberos (Session 54) as the authentication mechanism behind every SMB connection in a domain environment, which in turn depends on accurate time sync (Session 69).
Underlying storage (Session 77, SAN/NAS or local disk) with sufficient capacity, redundancy, and performance.
Network connectivity (Layer 3, Sessions 25–30) between clients and the server, including adequate bandwidth for the volume of file traffic.
Backup infrastructure (Session 78) to protect the data the file server holds.
dependents: What breaks, or degrades, if the file server is unavailable or misconfigured:
Every CEx agent trying to open a shared procedure document, escalation template, or scorecard — the shared drive simply doesn't appear or times out.
Any process or script (including scheduled tasks) that reads from or writes to a network share as part of its normal operation.
Compliance and audit processes that rely on centrally stored, access-controlled evidence rather than files scattered across individual laptops.
Onboarding/offboarding workflows — new hires can't get access to the resources they need if the underlying share and group structure isn't working correctly.

Home directories and redirected folders (Documents, Desktop) if the environment uses folder redirection, meaning a file server outage can look, to the end user, exactly like their entire profile is broken.
security: 8.1 Permission sprawl The most common real-world file server security problem isn't a sophisticated attack — it's years of ad- hoc permission grants ('just give Sarah access too, temporarily') that never get cleaned up, resulting in far more people having access to sensitive folders than should. Periodic access reviews (Section 4, step 8) are the primary defense, and are frequently a specific audit requirement in regulated industries.

8.2 Ransomware and file servers File servers are a prime ransomware target precisely because they're the central, shared repository — encrypting one file server can impact every department that relies on it. Defenses include the principle of least privilege (Session 85, minimizing who has write access to what), file screening (blocking known ransomware file extensions), Shadow Copies and proper backups (Session 78) as a recovery path, and monitoring for abnormal mass file-modification activity as an early detection signal.
Disable SMB1 entirely — it's legacy, insecure, and the protocol version associated with major exploits like EternalBlue.
Require SMB signing and, where performance allows, SMB encryption for sensitive shares.
Apply least-privilege NTFS permissions via groups rather than broad 'Everyone: Full Control' grants.
Enable object access auditing on sensitive shares so file access and modification is logged and feeds into centralized logging/SIEM (Sessions 82, 92).
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely cause First check User can't access a share they should have access to Missing from the correct AD security group, or NTFS/share permission mismatch Check effective permissions (icacls or Security tab 'Effective Access') and group membership.
'Access denied' despite having Full Control listed in share permissions More restrictive NTFS permission is overriding it Check NTFS permissions on the specific folder/file, not just the share.
Share is completely unreachable for everyone File server down, or DFS namespace pointing at a dead target Check server availability and DNS resolution; verify DFS target health.

Very slow file access over the network Bandwidth saturation, SMB version mismatch, or storage performance issue Check network utilization, confirm SMB version in use, check storage/disk latency on the server.

File suddenly missing or corrupted Accidental deletion/overwrite, or ransomware activity Check Shadow Copies/Previous Versions first for quick self-service recovery; escalate to backup restore and security investigation if pattern suggests ransomware.
example: Picture FundedNext onboarding a new batch of CEx agents. Each new hire is added to the CEx-Agents AD security group as part of the standard onboarding checklist, which automatically grants them read access to CEx-Docs (procedures, templates) and write access to their own scorecard subfolder — no one manually configures permissions per person, because the group-based model from Section 4 was set up correctly from the start.

A realistic incident on the same file server: a team lead reports that a specific escalation template 'looks wrong' compared to what other agents are seeing. Investigation shows two versions of the file exist because someone saved a personal copy locally, edited it, and re-uploaded it to the wrong subfolder rather than editing the authoritative version in place — a permissions/process issue rather than a technical failure, and a good illustration of why 'one authoritative shared location' (Section 1) only works if the workflow around it is followed, not just the technology itself.
cloud: Platform File server equivalent Key difference from on-prem AWS Amazon FSx (for Windows File Server, or FSx for NetApp ONTAP) Fully managed SMB file shares with AD integration, without administrators patching or maintaining the underlying servers.
Azure Azure Files SMB/NFS shares served directly from Azure Storage, mountable on-prem or in the cloud, with built-in redundancy options.
GCP Filestore Managed NFS file storage for workloads that need traditional file-share semantics rather than object storage.

Any cloud (SaaS layer) SharePoint Online / Google Drive / Google Workspace Shared Drives A more common modern replacement in many organizations — moves the model from network file shares to browser/app-based collaborative document storage entirely.

The conceptual shift moving to cloud: the core concept — one authoritative, permission-controlled, centrally backed-up location for shared files — doesn't change; what changes is who patches and maintains the underlying server, and increasingly, whether the access model is still SMB-share-based at all versus a SaaS collaboration platform like Google Workspace Shared Drives, which is conceptually closer to how the CEx team's Google Sheets-backed application already centralizes data.
automation: PowerShell is the primary automation surface on Windows file servers — Get-Acl / Set-Acl for permission auditing and changes, Get-SmbShare for enumerating shares, and New-SmbShare for provisioning new ones. A very common and genuinely valuable script is a scheduled permission-audit report: enumerate every group with access to a sensitive share, flag any individual users granted access directly (bypassing the group model), and email the result to the data owner — turning Section 8.1's 'permission sprawl' problem from a rare manual audit into an ongoing automated check.
This mirrors the same underlying instinct behind the internally built Google Apps Script CEx application:
rather than manually checking who has access to what, script the check and let it run on a schedule, surfacing anomalies before they become an audit finding or a security incident.
career: File servers are one of the most 'always there, always needed' pieces of enterprise infrastructure, which makes understanding permissions deeply — not just 'give them access' but why NTFS and share permissions interact the way they do — a genuinely high-value, frequently tested skill in both interviews and day-to-day support work.
Entry-level/help desk: resolve 'access denied' tickets correctly by checking both permission layers and group membership rather than guessing or over-granting access.
Sysadmin/network admin: design share and permission structures, manage DFS namespaces, implement quotas and Shadow Copies, run access reviews.
Security/compliance: audit permission sprawl, implement least-privilege models, respond to ransomware incidents involving shared storage.

This is also directly examinable material — NTFS vs. share permission interaction is a classic, frequently- tested topic in Windows Server administration certification tracks, and appears regularly in sysadmin interview questions.

misconceptions: “Give them Full Control on the share and they'll have full access.” — Only if NTFS permissions also allow it; the more restrictive of the two layers always wins (Section 3.2).

“Shadow Copies are a backup.” — They're a convenient, fast, self-service recovery mechanism for recent accidental changes, stored on the same volume — they don't protect against a full disk/server failure the way an actual backup (Session 78) does.

“Assigning permissions to individual users is fine for a small team.” — Even small teams grow and change; group-based permissions cost almost nothing extra to set up correctly at the start and save significant cleanup effort later.

“If the share is on the network, it must be secure.” — Network location says nothing about access control; a share with weak permissions is just as exposed as a public folder, regardless of where it physically lives.
anchors: “Most restrictive wins” — the one sentence that explains every confusing NTFS-vs-share permission ticket you'll ever troubleshoot.
Groups, not people — permissions go on AD security groups; people go in the groups. Never the other way around.
DFS = the 'one path, many possible servers behind it' trick — users never need to know which physical server they're actually talking to.
Shadow Copy = self-service time machine for one file; Backup = the real safety net for the whole server.
connections: File servers are the clearest demonstration yet of how Layer 4 (Identity) underpins Layer 5 (Enterprise Services): every permission decision on this session's topic traces directly back to Active Directory users and groups from Sessions 51–52 and 22, and every authenticated connection depends on Kerberos (Session 54) and, transitively, NTP (Session 69) for that authentication to succeed at all.
Session 22 (Groups) — the direct mechanism every NTFS permission structure in this session is built on.
Sessions 51–52 (Directory Services, Active Directory) and Session 54 (Kerberos) — identity and authentication underpinning every file access.
Session 67 (DNS) and Session 69 (NTP) — name resolution and time sync, both silent prerequisites for SMB/Kerberos to work at all.
Session 68 (DHCP) — same layer, same 'invisible until broken' character as this session's topic.

Looking ahead: Session 77 (Storage, SAN/NAS) covers the underlying storage layer file servers sit on top of; Session 78 (Backup) covers how that data is protected long-term; Session 85 (Least Privilege), later in Layer 6, formalizes the permission-design philosophy introduced here.

lab: Home/virtualized lab — build a small permission model and deliberately reproduce the most common real-world file server tickets.
17.On a Windows Server VM (ideally joined to a lab AD domain from earlier sessions), create a folder and share it, e.g., CEx-Docs.
18.Create two AD security groups, CEx-ReadOnly and CEx-Modify, and add a test user account to each.
19.Set NTFS permissions on the folder: CEx-ReadOnly = Read, CEx-Modify = Modify. Leave share permissions at Everyone: Full Control (Section 3.2 best practice).
20.Log in as each test user and confirm the read-only user cannot save changes, while the modify user can — this directly demonstrates the 'most restrictive wins' rule in the diagram above.
21.Enable Shadow Copies on the volume, edit a test file, then use 'Previous Versions' to restore an earlier copy without touching backup software.

22.Deliberately misconfigure it: set the share permission to Read Only while leaving NTFS at Full Control, and confirm even the Modify-group user is now blocked — reproducing the most common 'access denied despite correct-looking permissions' ticket from Section 9.
23.Optional stretch goal: if you have a second file server VM, set up a DFS Namespace pointing to the same share on both, and practice failing over from one target to the other.
